They said that they occupied a middle position between the determinists and the Muʿtazilites.
Human actions, they argued, are created by God. Human beings cannot create any of those actions themselves.
But even if people cannot create their actions, they can still “acquire” them.

The Andalusian Ẓāhirī thinker Ibn Ḥazm, who died in 456 AH, rightly argued that this position does not differ in any essential way from determinism because it never clearly establishes genuine human choice.
The Ashʿarites say that God creates both the act and the ability to perform it in the human being.
The person then directs that act as they wish, toward good or evil, and in this way earns either reward or punishment.
This would seem to make people responsible for what they do because they have freedom of choice.
But Ashʿarite atomism creates a serious problem for this position.

According to their atomist doctrine, substances and their accidents are constantly changing and continually coming into existence, while God directly and continuously creates both the substances and their accidents.
This undermines the very freedom of choice the Ashʿarites claim to preserve.
If God is continuously and directly involved in every human act and every human movement, then human freedom becomes impossible to maintain in any real sense.
4 — The advocates of Ashʿarite atomism also tried to follow what they presented as a “rational” path.
Through this method, they tried to prove that substances and their qualities ultimately come from nothing—that is, from non-being—and are therefore created in time.
The world, which is made up of atoms, or these individual substances that cannot be divided any further, must therefore also have been created in time.
But although this method looked “rational” in form, they departed from the substance of rationalism in two ways.
First, they rejected reason’s conception of the qualities of individual substances. They denied those qualities when they were known through reason.
Second, they rejected the objective existence of the qualities and accidents carried by those individual substances, while at the same time treating the mind itself as the source of their existence.
5 — When the Ashʿarites spoke about causation, they said that God is the direct cause of every change that occurs in substances and accidents.
There is no other cause in the universe apart from this direct cause, which is God.
They based this on one of the supposedly “rational” principles of their school: an accident does not remain for two moments.
At every moment, therefore, a new accident appears and requires a new act of creation by the same direct cause: God.
This Ashʿarite position leads directly to an irrational conclusion.
It denies the laws of nature and society altogether and removes any basis on which a scientific system can be built in any field of knowledge.
The final result is to destroy one of the necessary foundations for the development of society itself.
Here the signs of the ideological struggle become clearer and clearer.
This was the struggle that reached one stage under the leadership of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī at the end of the third Islamic century, and another under al-Ghazālī at the end of the fifth.

One revealing example of this ideological struggle is the well-known fact that al-Ghazālī wrote his famous book The Scandals of the Bāṭinites at the request of the Abbasid caliph al-Mustaẓhir, who came to power in 487 AH/1094 CE.
Al-Ghazālī even gave the work the alternative title al-Mustaẓhirī.
This was one form of the alliance between Ashʿarite kalām and official state thought.

Facing them in the ideological struggle was a broad opposing camp made up of a mixture of social and intellectual forces that were hostile to—or at least opposed to—the direction taken by the ruling power.
The Shia played an important role both in the rise of kalām and in the later development of its debates.
But in our present discussion, we cannot include every group that has been called “Shia” in Islamic history.
If we tried to cover the full historical meaning of the term in all its different uses, we would enter a maze with no clear way out.
We will therefore limit ourselves to its best-known meaning: the Twelver Imami Shia.
There are two sides to the Imami Shia’s role in kalām.
The first is the specifically doctrinal side of Shiism itself.

The second concerns the contributions of theologians who belonged to the Imami school and who played an important part in developing the questions discussed in kalām at different stages in its history.
A — The doctrinal side: If we look only at the doctrine itself, we can say that many of the principles on which Imami Shiism is built are also major subjects of kalām.
Some are directly connected to the great political questions that drove the earliest political conflicts from the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs onward.

These include the question of the caliphate; the question of the person who commits a major sin, which arose partly from the killing of the third Rightly Guided Caliph, ʿUthmān; the question of how to deal with an unjust ruler; and the duty to command what is right and forbid what is wrong.
Other theological questions appeared later as the earlier political conflict continued and intensified, while ideological positions were reformulated in new and more developed intellectual forms.
These included divine decree and predestination, human freedom, the concepts of divine unity and justice, faith, the theory of knowledge, and the status of reason.
On all these disputed questions, the Imamis developed views and positions that formed both the structure of Shiite doctrine and the structure of Shiite kalām.
If we look at Shiite kalām in broad terms, we find that the Twelver Imamis took some positions that were unique to them.
The clearest example is the caliphate.
Unlike either the Ashʿarites or the Muʿtazilites, they regarded the caliphate as a divine right belonging to the person whom God chooses for it.

They believed this divine right belonged to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and then to his descendants through his wife Fāṭima, the daughter of the Prophet, in a direct line down to the twelfth Imam, Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan.
They also believed that the Imam who possesses this right is protected from error.
On some other questions, the Imamis agreed with the Ashʿarites rather than the Muʿtazilites.
One example is the status of a Muslim who commits a major sin.
Like the Ashʿarites, the Imamis say that such a person remains a believer but is sinful and deserves punishment in proportion to the sin.
The Muʿtazilites, by contrast, say that this person is neither a believer nor an unbeliever, but occupies a position between belief and unbelief.
The Kharijites say that such a person is an unbeliever.
The Imamis also agree with the Ashʿarites on the interpretation of religious texts—the Qurʾān and Sunna—when their apparent meaning conflicts with reason.
Like the Ashʿarites, they allow interpretation when the plain meaning of a text conflicts with the most basic judgments of reason.
Outside such cases, they do not favor this approach.
They hold that religious knowledge remains the basic authority, rather than the judgment of reason.
On still other questions, the Imamis agree with the Muʿtazilites rather than the Ashʿarites.
One example is the question of whether reason itself can recognize good and evil.
Like the Muʿtazilites, the Imamis believe that some actions and things are good or bad in themselves and that reason can recognize this.
In other words, goodness and badness exist objectively in such actions and things.
They are not good or bad only because religious law declares them so.
The question of human freedom remains.
What is the Shiite position on whether people freely choose their actions?
On this important question, their position is based on a saying attributed to the sixth of the Twelve Imams, Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq:
“Neither compulsion nor delegation, but something between the two.”
The Shia explain this by saying that human actions must be looked at from two directions: their immediate causes and their more distant causes.
If we look at the immediate causes, the human being is the direct cause of the action.
The action comes from the person by choice.
From this point of view, the person is responsible for whether the act is good or evil.
But if we look at the more distant causes, we find that these lie outside the person’s own will and choice.
They are necessary conditions, and from this point of view the action cannot simply be attributed to the person alone.
In the Shiite explanation, a person’s ability to perform an action belongs to these more distant causes.
That ability is something God created in the person.
Human actions are therefore created by God in the sense that God created the power that makes them possible.
But they are also created by the human being in the sense that the person directly performs them by an act of will.

The position is therefore presented as a middle ground between the Ashʿarites, who say that people do not truly possess their actions or determine their fate, and the Muʿtazilites, who say that people determine their own fate without the Creator exercising any influence over their actions.
More generally, we often find the Shia occupying a middle position between the Ashʿarites and the Muʿtazilites in kalām.
The deeper explanation for this “middle position” may lie in the extremely difficult historical situation the Shia faced over several centuries.
They were repeatedly forced into painful forms of conflict.
At times they confronted their opponents openly and firmly.
At other times they relied on taqiyya—protective concealment—combined with withdrawal.
At still other times they used concealment while continuing their opposition in secret.
Throughout all this, they suffered terrible disasters, including at times physical destruction on a large scale.
If we try to identify the ideology of Shiism as a whole simply from the theory of Shiism itself, we quickly find ourselves inside a closed circle of contradictions.
One of the clearest contradictions can be seen by comparing two sets of Shiite positions.

On one side is the theory of the Imamate: the belief that the caliphate is purely a divine right, the denial of the people’s right to choose the caliph, the belief that the Imam is protected from error, and the restriction of the source of religious knowledge after the Prophet to the Imam.
On the other side are the Shiite positions on human freedom and on reason’s ability to recognize good and evil.
We can draw the following conclusion.
The first set of positions belongs to the original foundation of Shiite doctrine.
